name: Jobs-to-be-Done interview
what: A timeline interview that reconstructs a specific past purchase or switch: the first thought, the trigger event, the search, the anxieties, and the moment of decision. It surfaces the functional, emotional and social 'job' the product was hired for, and the forces that pushed and held the person back.
qs: What triggered the last switch to an alternative in this category?
What job is the customer really hiring this product to do?
Which anxieties or habits block a switch even when the offer is better?
What did they compare against at the moment of purchase?

name: Contextual interview
what: An interview conducted in the place where the behaviour actually happens — the kitchen, the shop floor, the workshop — combining questions with a live walkthrough of the task. Physical evidence in the environment corrects what people misremember or edit.
qs: How is the task really performed, step by step, in the real setting?
Which constraints of the space, equipment or workflow will our product hit?
Where do improvised fixes and workarounds appear?
What do they own or store already that competes with our product?

name: Ethnographic observation
what: Extended, low-intervention observation of a group in its natural setting — a market, a canteen, a repair café — recording behaviour, sequences and social rules without asking questions. Used to find needs people cannot articulate because the behaviour is habitual.
qs: What do people actually do, as opposed to what they say they do?
Which unspoken norms or rituals govern behaviour in this setting?
Where does friction appear that nobody complains about?
Are there recurring patterns across sites that a product could serve?

name: Shadowing
what: Following one person through a whole task or shift and recording each step, decision, interruption and handover. Useful for operator-facing and B2B ideas where the buyer's real workflow determines whether a product can be adopted.
qs: How much time does the target task consume in a real day?
Where in the workflow would our product have to be inserted?
Who else touches the process and must agree to a change?
What interruptions or constraints would break our assumed usage flow?

name: Customer journey mapping
what: Reconstructing the end-to-end sequence a customer passes through — trigger, search, evaluation, purchase, use, repeat — from interview and observation data, and marking pains, drop-offs and moments of truth. It is a synthesis method, so its quality depends entirely on the field data behind it.
qs: Where exactly do customers drop out of the current journey?
Which touchpoint carries the most emotion or risk?
Which stage should the first experiment target?
Do different segments follow materially different journeys?

name: Diary study
what: Participants log the relevant behaviour themselves over days or weeks, prompted by a short daily template. It captures frequency, context and variation that a single interview compresses or loses.
qs: How often does the need actually arise over a normal week?
In which contexts and at which times does it cluster?
How stable is the behaviour, or does novelty fade after a few days?
What situational triggers precede the behaviour?

name: Photo/video diary
what: A diary study where participants capture images or short clips instead of text — the fridge, the shelf, the workbench, the plate. Visual evidence exposes brands, quantities, storage and mess that written entries omit.
qs: What do people actually have on hand, and in what condition?
How is the product stored, prepared or displayed in reality?
Which competing items sit alongside ours in the same moment?
Does the real portion, format or setting match our design assumption?

name: Experience sampling
what: Short prompts sent at random or event-triggered moments asking what the person is doing and feeling right now. It samples in-the-moment states rather than recalled summaries, giving better frequency and intensity estimates.
qs: How intense is the need at the moment it occurs, not in hindsight?
What is the real incidence rate of the trigger situation per person per week?
Which moments of the day are the strongest occasions for our offer?
Does self-reported importance match how often it actually comes up?

name: Day-in-the-life study
what: A full-day observation or reconstruction of a target customer's routine, mapping where the category fits among competing demands on time, money and attention. Especially useful for occasion-driven food, retail and hospitality concepts.
qs: Which occasion in the day does our concept realistically occupy?
What else competes for that same slot and budget?
What time and energy does the customer actually have at that moment?
Where in the day is the natural point of purchase?

name: Extreme-user interview
what: Interviews with people at the far ends of the usage distribution — heaviest users, most constrained, most improvisational. Their exaggerated workarounds make latent needs visible that mainstream users have quietly accepted.
qs: What do heavy or constrained users build for themselves today?
Which requirement becomes obvious only at the extreme?
Is the extreme need a preview of a mainstream need or a niche?
What would make a heavy user abandon their current workaround?

name: Lead-user research
what: Identifying users who are ahead of the market and have already modified or self-built a solution, then studying their prototypes and reasoning. Common in crafts, hardware and specialty food, where enthusiasts innovate before suppliers do.
qs: Has anyone already built a version of this themselves, and how?
Which features did lead users prioritise when free to choose?
Is the lead-user need trending toward the mainstream?
Could a lead user become a first customer, tester or co-developer?

name: Non-user research
what: Interviews with people who fit the target profile but deliberately do not use the category, to find the real barriers — price, access, distrust, ritual, identity. Non-users define the ceiling of the market far better than enthusiasts do.
qs: Why do qualified people not buy in this category at all?
Is the barrier price, access, habit, trust or identity?
Is the non-user segment large enough to be a growth target?
Which barrier could a product realistically remove?

name: Lapsed-customer interview
what: Interviews with people who bought or visited and then stopped, to isolate the cause of churn. It gives sharper signal than satisfaction surveys because the decision has already been made and paid for.
qs: Why did customers stop buying or visiting after trying us?
Was the failure product, price, convenience or service?
What would have to change for them to return?
Did they switch to a substitute or leave the category?

name: Lost-sale interview
what: A short structured conversation with prospects who engaged but did not buy, run close to the decision so the reasoning is fresh. Reveals whether the block was offer, price, trust, timing or a competitor.
qs: What was the actual reason this prospect did not buy?
Which alternative did they choose instead, and why?
Was our price the barrier or the justification for it?
At which step of the sale did they disengage?

name: Win/loss interview
what: Paired interviews across both won and lost deals using the same question set, so the differences between them can be compared systematically. Mostly used for B2B, wholesale and retailer listings.
qs: What distinguishes buyers who said yes from those who said no?
Which decision criteria dominated the choice?
Which of our claims were believed and which were discounted?
Who in the buying group actually decided?

name: Complaint mining
what: Systematic coding of complaints — ours or competitors' — from service logs, hotline records, retailer feedback or social channels, into recurring problem categories with frequency counts. Cheap access to real, unsolicited pain.
qs: Which failure modes do customers complain about most often?
Are complaints about the product, the service or the expectation set?
Which competitor weakness is complained about consistently enough to attack?
How often does a complaint end in churn?

name: Search-intent research
what: Analysis of search volumes, query phrasing, seasonality and geography for problem, category and competitor terms. It measures whether demand is already being expressed in words, and in which words.
qs: Is anyone actively searching for a solution to this problem?
Which vocabulary does the market use — ours or a different one?
How seasonal or regional is the demand?
Which adjacent queries reveal the real jobs being done?

name: Community/forum research
what: Reading and coding discussions in the places the target group already gathers — subreddits, trade forums, Facebook groups, association mailing lists, local WhatsApp groups. Also identifies where a first audience could be recruited.
qs: What problems does this community raise on its own, unprompted?
Which vocabulary, references and authorities does it trust?
Are there recurring recommendation requests we could answer?
Is this community reachable as a first channel?

name: Expert interview
what: Structured conversations with people who have run the specific business type before — chefs, buyers, plant managers, regulators, master craftspeople — to test feasibility and cost assumptions fast. Experts predict operations and constraints well but market demand poorly.
qs: Is this technically and operationally feasible as specified?
Which cost, yield or regulatory assumption is naive?
What kills most ventures of this type in the first year?
What would an experienced operator do differently and why?

name: Stakeholder interview
what: Interviews with the non-customer parties whose consent the venture needs — landlords, municipalities, partners, investors, neighbours, works councils. It maps the approvals and interests that can block an otherwise valid concept.
qs: Whose approval is required before this can operate?
What are the stated and unstated interests of each party?
Which stakeholder can block the project outright?
What conditions would each attach to a yes?

name: Supply-chain interview
what: Conversations with suppliers, co-packers, wholesalers, logistics providers and distributors about availability, minimums, lead times, seasonality and price steps. Often the fastest way to find that a concept is economically impossible before spending on product.
qs: Can the required input be sourced reliably at the volume we need?
What are the real minimum order quantities and lead times?
How volatile is input price and availability across the year?
Which margin does each intermediary expect to take?

name: Analogous-market research
what: Studying a different market, geography or category where a structurally similar model already works, and extracting the mechanisms, economics and failure patterns. Substitutes for direct evidence when the local market has no precedent.
qs: Has this model already been proven somewhere else, and under what conditions?
Which of those conditions exist in our market and which do not?
What unit economics does the analogue achieve at maturity?
What went wrong for the ones that failed?

name: Concept board test
what: A visual version of the concept card — image, packaging or venue visual plus a short claim — tested for appeal and comprehension. Adds the visual dimension that written concepts miss, which matters for food, retail and craft products.
qs: Does the visual communicate the intended category and quality level?
Do the image and the claim reinforce or contradict each other?
What do people assume about price from the visual alone?
Which visual element carries the appeal?

name: Multiple-concept test
what: Several concepts shown to the same respondents in one session so they can be compared directly and ranked. Fast way to narrow a portfolio, though direct comparison inflates the differences between options.
qs: Which of our candidate concepts is strongest with the target group?
Do different segments prefer different concepts?
Is there a clear winner or are all concepts equally weak?
Which concept elements can be recombined into a stronger one?

name: Monadic concept test
what: Each respondent sees exactly one concept and rates it without any comparison, mimicking the real market where a customer meets one offer at a time. Cleaner absolute scores, but needs a larger sample.
qs: How does this concept score on its own, without a comparison crutch?
Does it beat our category norm or benchmark for purchase intent?
Is appeal driven by the concept itself or by contrast effects?
How does the absolute score vary by segment?

name: Sequential monadic test
what: Respondents evaluate several concepts one after another, each fully rated before the next appears, with rotated order to control position bias. Combines absolute scoring with within-respondent comparison at a manageable sample size.
qs: How do concepts rank once each is judged on its own merits?
Does order of exposure change the verdict?
Which concept holds up after respondents have seen alternatives?
Are the differences between concepts large enough to act on?

name: Concept ranking
what: Respondents place a set of concepts in preference order, optionally with a reason for first and last place. Very quick to run and analyse; tells you order but not the size of the gaps or whether anyone would buy at all.
qs: What is the relative preference order across our concept set?
Which concept is consistently rejected?
Do rankings differ systematically between segments?
What reasons do people give for their first and last choice?

name: Concept sorting
what: Respondents group concepts or attributes into piles of their own or a given definition, revealing the mental categories they use. Useful for deciding what the offer will be seen as competing with.
qs: Which category do customers file our concept under?
Which products do they see as our real substitutes?
Which attributes do they treat as belonging together?
Does our intended positioning survive their categorisation?

name: Forced-choice concept test
what: Respondents must pick one option from a set with no 'all of them' or 'none' escape, replicating the trade-off of a real purchase. Removes the polite over-rating typical of scale questions.
qs: When forced to choose, which concept wins?
Which trade-off are customers willing to accept?
Does our concept beat the leading incumbent head-to-head?
Which attribute is sacrificed first under constraint?

name: MaxDiff concept test
what: Respondents repeatedly pick the best and worst item from small rotating subsets, producing a scaled importance ranking across many concepts or features. Discriminates far better than rating scales when the list is long.
qs: Which features or claims matter most and least, on a common scale?
How large is the gap between the top and second attribute?
Do importance scores differ by segment?
Which attributes can be dropped without losing appeal?

name: Concept “sell me this” test
what: The respondent is asked to explain the concept back and pitch it to someone else as if recommending it. Fluent, enthusiastic re-selling is a strong signal of comprehension and word-of-mouth potential; hesitation exposes a muddled proposition.
qs: Can a customer explain the offer accurately to a third party?
Which benefit do they lead with when they retell it?
Is the proposition memorable enough to be passed on?
Where does the retelling drop or distort the key claim?

name: Concept comprehension test
what: A check of whether the concept, claim or label is understood as intended, using unaided playback and targeted probes. Run before any appeal measurement, since a misunderstood concept produces meaningless scores.
qs: What do people think this product actually is and does?
Which words or claims are misread?
Do they understand how and when to use it?
Does comprehension differ across languages or regions?

name: Concept association test
what: Free or prompted association of words, feelings and imagery with the concept, name or visual. Surfaces unintended connotations early, which matters in multilingual markets and for craft, health or provenance claims.
qs: Which associations does the concept trigger spontaneously?
Are there negative or off-category associations we must avoid?
Does the concept evoke the intended quality and price tier?
Do associations hold across the languages we will trade in?

name: Benefit prioritization test
what: Customers rank or allocate points across the candidate benefits of the offer, establishing which promise should lead the communication. Directly feeds packaging, menu and landing-page copy.
qs: Which single benefit should headline the proposition?
Which benefits are merely expected and earn no preference?
Do priorities differ between buyer and end user?
Which benefit is worth paying more for?

name: Problem-solution fit test
what: A structured session in which the previously validated problem is restated to the customer and the proposed solution is presented against it, checking whether the solution is seen as addressing the pain that was actually described. Bridges discovery and concept work.
qs: Do customers accept that our solution addresses their stated problem?
Which part of the problem does the solution leave untouched?
Is our solution better than the workaround they already use?
Would they change behaviour for this improvement?

name: Concept + competitor test
what: The concept is presented alongside the real alternatives the customer would face, at their real prices, and the customer chooses. Approximates the shelf or the high street far better than a solo concept test.
qs: Would customers choose us over the actual alternatives available today?
Which competitor is the real reference point?
Is our differentiation visible without being explained?
What price gap to the incumbent can we sustain?

name: Concept co-creation workshop
what: A facilitated session in which target customers help shape the concept — configuring the offer, menu, format or packaging from components. Produces ideas and priorities, not validation, since participants are self-selected and engaged.
qs: Which configuration do customers build when they are free to choose?
Which elements do they add and which do they delete?
Where does the group disagree, indicating separate segments?
Which assumptions of ours do they never mention at all?

name: Crowdsourced ideation
what: Opening idea generation to a wider community — customers, staff, an online crowd, a competition — with a defined brief and selection criteria. Broadens the option set cheaply; the resulting ideas still need testing.
qs: Which solution directions do people outside the team see?
Which recurring idea appears independently from many contributors?
Is there latent enthusiasm and a potential first audience here?
Which ideas are feasible within our real constraints?

name: Name test
what: Candidate names are tested with the target group for pronounceability, recall, meaning, connotation and legal/linguistic risk, ideally in every language the business will trade in. Cheap to run and expensive to skip, since the name is embedded in signage, packaging and domains.
qs: Is the name understood, pronounceable and memorable in each market language?
Does it signal the intended category and quality tier?
Does it carry an unintended or offensive meaning anywhere we will trade?
Which name is recalled unaided a day later?

name: Naming A/B test
what: Two or more names are run live against real traffic — ads, landing pages, market-stall signage — and compared on click, sign-up or purchase rather than opinion. Turns a taste argument into a behavioural measurement.
qs: Which name produces more clicks, sign-ups or sales in the real channel?
Is the difference large enough to matter, or noise?
Does the winning name attract the segment we want?
Does the name change cost per acquisition?

name: Logo test
what: Logo and identity options are tested for legibility at real sizes and distances, category fit, perceived price tier and emotional read. For physical businesses the test should include the actual application — awning, jar, apron, van.
qs: Is the mark legible at shopfront and label size?
What price tier and category does the identity imply?
Does it stand apart from the local competitive set?
Which associations does it trigger before any text is read?

name: Packaging mockup test
what: Realistic dummy packs are shown or handled by target customers to test comprehension, appeal, perceived value and standout. Best run with physical mockups rather than screen renders, since material, weight and finish carry much of the signal.
qs: Does the pack communicate what the product is within a few seconds?
What price would customers expect from this pack?
Does the pack feel consistent with our quality claim in the hand?
Which on-pack element is read first?

name: Shelf simulation
what: The pack is placed among real competitor packs on a mocked-up or real shelf, and shoppers are asked to find, choose or notice it under time pressure. It measures standout in context rather than appeal in isolation.
qs: Is our pack found within a realistic browsing time?
Does it stand out against the actual competitive set?
Which shelf position and facing count does it need to work?
Is it mistaken for a competitor or a different category?

name: Shelf-eye-tracking test
what: Eye-tracking hardware or software records fixation order, dwell time and areas of no attention while shoppers scan a shelf. Objective attention data, but attention is not purchase and the lab setting inflates engagement.
qs: Is our pack seen at all during a normal scan?
Which on-pack element captures first fixation?
How long is the pack looked at relative to competitors?
Which claims are never read?

name: First-impression test
what: A pack, storefront, menu or page is shown for a few seconds and then hidden, after which the viewer reports what it was, what it offered and how it felt. Replicates the very short attention real customers give.
qs: What is understood in the first five seconds?
Which single message survives a glance?
Is the category immediately clear?
What is remembered and what is lost?

name: Message test
what: Alternative claims, straplines or descriptions are tested for clarity, believability and motivating power, either in a survey or live in ads. Separates messages people like from messages that move them.
qs: Which message is most believable to a sceptical customer?
Which claim actually motivates a next step?
Are any claims dismissed as exaggerated?
Does the winning message work in all our languages?

name: Positioning test
what: A full positioning statement — target, frame of reference, differentiator, reason to believe — is presented and probed for credibility and relevance against the alternatives customers already know. Tests the strategy, not the wording.
qs: Do customers accept our claimed point of difference?
Is the frame of reference we chose the one they use?
Is our reason to believe convincing without a demo?
Does the positioning make the price feel justified?

name: Price-image test
what: Customers estimate the price of the product from the name, pack, venue or visual alone, before any price is disclosed. The gap between the guessed price and the intended price shows whether the design supports the pricing strategy.
qs: What price does the design lead customers to expect?
Is our intended price above or below the perceived value?
Which design cues drive the price read up or down?
Does the price image match the positioning we intend?

name: Packaging comprehension test
what: A focused check on whether mandatory and functional pack information — variety, quantity, usage, preparation, allergens, storage — is found and correctly understood. Errors here create returns, complaints and compliance exposure.
qs: Do customers correctly identify variety, size and usage from the pack?
Is the preparation or storage instruction found and understood?
Are legally required elements noticed?
Does anything on the pack create a false expectation?

name: Packaging usability test
what: Real users open, dose, reseal, store and dispose of the pack while being observed, with time and error recorded. Physical failures — hard to open, leaks, does not reclose, does not fit the shelf — are found only this way.
qs: Can the target user open the pack without tools or spillage?
Does the closure work reliably after repeated use?
Does the pack fit real fridges, shelves and cupboards?
Can users dispose of or sort the materials correctly?

name: Unboxing test
what: The first-contact sequence — outer carton, protection, reveal, inserts, waste — is observed and recorded as it happens, usually filmed. Relevant for direct-to-consumer, gifting and premium craft products where the first minute carries the quality verdict.
qs: Does the first physical impression match the promised quality tier?
Does the product arrive undamaged and correctly presented?
Which step of the reveal creates delight or irritation?
Is the packaging waste seen as excessive?

name: Landing-page test
what: A single page presents the offer, the benefit and a clear call to action, with traffic driven from ads, flyers, QR codes or a community post; conversion on the call to action is the measured variable. This is the canonical form of the smoke test — advertising an offer as if it existed and measuring the response before anything is built.
qs: What share of qualified visitors take the requested action?
Which value proposition converts best?
What does an acquired lead cost through this channel?
Which objections show up in the messages people send?

name: Waitlist test
what: Interested people leave contact details to be notified at launch, giving a low-friction commitment signal and a real audience to activate later. Sign-up is weak evidence on its own, so it is usually the first step of a two-stage test.
qs: How many people will give an email address for this offer?
How fast does the list grow per unit of promotion?
Which sources produce the highest-quality sign-ups?
How many waitlist members later convert when asked to pay?

name: Pre-order test
what: Customers place a real, paid order for a product that does not exist yet, with a stated delivery date and refund policy. Run as a single test it measures whether money moves before production; run as a time-boxed campaign with a target and a promotional plan it also tests the whole go-to-market machine. Money changing hands before production is one of the strongest early demand signals available.
qs: Will customers pay in advance for an unbuilt product?
What conversion rate does the offer achieve at the intended price?
How many pre-orders can we generate per week per channel?
What refund or cancellation rate do we see before delivery?

name: Deposit / prepayment test
what: Customers transfer real money — a partial payment or a full prepayment — to reserve a unit, slot or place before it exists. Variants differ only in how much is asked: a token deposit lowers the barrier, a full prepayment gives the strongest signal and funds the build. Common for made-to-order craft goods, equipment and hospitality bookings.
qs: Will customers commit money before the product exists?
What deposit size can we ask before conversion collapses?
How many deposits convert to full payment at delivery?
Which customer type is willing to reserve?

name: Crowdfunding test
what: A public campaign with tiers, a target and a deadline tests demand, price ladder and story simultaneously, while raising working capital. Strong evidence, but it measures the appeal of a campaign to a platform audience, not steady retail demand.
qs: Will strangers fund this product before it exists?
Which reward tier and price point sells best?
Does the story travel beyond our own network?
What does a backer cost to acquire?

name: Concierge MVP
what: The service is delivered manually and personally to a small number of real, paying customers, with the founder doing every step by hand. The point is to learn the real process and the real value before automating or investing in equipment.
qs: Will customers pay for the outcome when it is delivered by hand?
What does one delivery actually take in time, cost and steps?
Which part of the promised value do customers care about most?
Which steps could later be standardised or removed?

name: Wizard-of-Oz prototype
what: The customer experiences what looks like a finished, automated product while humans perform the work invisibly behind it. It tests demand and experience without building the machinery, kitchen or system.
qs: Do customers use and value the experience when it appears finished?
What is the real workload behind each transaction?
Which steps must be automated first to be viable?
Where does the illusion break under real usage?

name: Mechanical-Turk prototype
what: A variant of Wizard-of-Oz in which the hidden manual work is distributed to a pool of people or freelancers rather than the founder. Lets the test scale to more customers before any automation exists.
qs: Can the manual process handle real volume?
What is the marginal cost per order when humans do the work?
Does quality stay consistent across different operators?
At what volume does manual delivery break down?

name: Pinocchio prototype
what: A non-functional physical stand-in — a wooden block, a dummy jar, a mocked-up machine — is carried, placed or used in the real environment to test form, size and habit. Named for the wooden model used before any working parts exist.
qs: Is the size, weight and form right for real use and storage?
Would the object fit the space and routine it is meant for?
How often would it be reached for in a normal week?
Which physical dimension needs to change before we tool up?

name: Role-play prototype
what: Team members act out the customer-facing service end to end with real people in the role of customers, in the real or a mocked-up space. Exposes scripts, handovers and awkward moments before any fit-out spend.
qs: Does the service sequence make sense to a first-time customer?
Where does the interaction stall or confuse?
How long does each step really take?
Which staff role is overloaded?

name: Service-theater test
what: A full staged run of the service in a realistic set — a borrowed room dressed as the venue, a stall dressed as the shop — with real customers and props but no permanent investment. A dress rehearsal that produces genuine reactions.
qs: Does the whole experience hold together for a paying guest?
Which atmosphere elements actually carry the concept?
Where do customers hesitate or need help?
What must be fixed before committing to a lease or fit-out?

name: Manual back-office MVP
what: The customer-facing offer is real, while ordering, scheduling, invoicing and stock behind it are handled on paper, spreadsheets and messages. Defers all systems investment until volume proves it is needed.
qs: Can we serve real customers before building systems?
Which back-office step consumes the most time per order?
At what volume does the manual approach break?
Which process should be systematised first?

name: Prototype-as-product test
what: An early, imperfect prototype is sold as the actual product to a small set of tolerant customers who know its status. Generates revenue and real-use data, and tests whether the core value survives rough edges.
qs: Will customers pay for the product in its current imperfect state?
Which flaws are tolerated and which are deal-breakers?
What does real use reveal that testing did not?
Do early buyers repeat or recommend?

name: Sketch test
what: A hand-drawn or quickly rendered depiction of the product, space or menu is shown to customers to test the idea before any model is made. The roughness invites criticism that polished renders suppress.
qs: Is the idea understood from a rough drawing alone?
Which element do people react to first?
What do they assume is missing or wrong?
Is it worth building a physical model of this direction?

name: Paper prototype
what: Flat paper or card representations of a product, label, menu or interface are made in minutes and walked through with users. Almost free, and it keeps attention on structure and sequence rather than finish.
qs: Is the intended structure, layout or sequence understood?
Which information is missing at each step?
Which variant of the layout do users follow correctly?
Is the concept worth a physical model?

name: Cardboard prototype
what: Full-scale card mock-ups of products, fixtures, packaging or even room layouts, cut and taped to real dimensions. Cheap way to test size, reach and spatial fit before any material or joinery spend.
qs: Are the dimensions right in the real space?
Can people reach, lift, stack or pass it as intended?
Does the layout work for staff and customer movement?
Which measurement needs to change before we build?

name: Foam prototype
what: Shaped foam models used to evaluate volume, proportion, grip and silhouette by hand. Standard step in consumer hardware and housewares before any tooling decision.
qs: Does the form feel right in the hand?
Is the proportion and volume correct for the intended use?
Which shape variant do users prefer to hold?
Where does the geometry need adjusting?

name: CNC prototype
what: A subtractively machined prototype in a production-like material, giving realistic stiffness, weight, finish and fit. Slower and more expensive than printing, but far closer to the real part.
qs: Does the part behave correctly in a production-grade material?
Is the surface finish and weight acceptable to customers?
Do the tolerances hold in the real material?
Is the design manufacturable as drawn?

name: Prototype machining run
what: A short run of parts made on production-representative equipment to test repeatability, cycle time and cost per part. The bridge between one-off prototypes and a manufacturing decision.
qs: Can the part be made repeatably within tolerance?
What is the real cycle time and cost per unit at this stage?
Which features drive the cost or scrap rate?
What tooling investment would production require?

name: Appearance prototype
what: A non-functional model built to production appearance — colour, material, finish, graphics — used for customer response, photography and buyer meetings. It tests desirability while engineering continues separately.
qs: Does the product look like the quality tier we claim?
Which colour and finish combination is preferred?
Does it photograph and present well to buyers?
What price does its appearance imply?

name: Functional prototype
what: A working unit that performs the core function, even if it looks unfinished, used to verify that the central technical promise holds. Separates 'it works' from 'it looks right', which should be tested independently.
qs: Does the core function work as specified?
What performance level does it actually achieve?
Which component limits performance?
Is the technical concept viable at all?

name: Ergonomic prototype
what: A prototype evaluated for posture, reach, grip force, comfort and fatigue with a range of body types, often over a realistic use duration. Essential for tools, equipment, furniture and back-of-house kit.
qs: Is the product comfortable to use over a realistic session?
Does it work for the range of body sizes and strengths in our users?
Where does discomfort or fatigue appear first?
Is one-handed or gloved use possible where needed?

name: Destructive prototype test
what: The product is loaded, bent, crushed or cycled until it fails, and the failure point and mode are recorded. Establishes the real safety margin rather than the calculated one.
qs: At what load or cycle count does the product fail?
Which component fails first, and how?
Is the safety margin adequate for real misuse?
Which design change raises the failure threshold most cheaply?

name: Stress test
what: The product or system is run at or beyond its rated conditions — load, temperature, duty cycle, throughput — to see where performance degrades. Applies to equipment, packaging and to operational systems alike.
qs: Does performance hold at the top of the rated range?
Where does the first degradation appear?
What margin exists between normal and failing conditions?
Which failure is graceful and which is catastrophic?

name: Drop test
what: Standardised drops from defined heights onto defined surfaces, in defined orientations, with damage assessed after each. Standard for packaging, glassware, appliances and anything shipped.
qs: Does the product survive realistic drops in transit and in use?
Which orientation is most vulnerable?
Is the protective packaging adequate?
What damage rate should we expect in distribution?

name: Transport simulation
what: Vibration, compression, stacking and climate cycles replicating a real shipping lane, run on a packed pallet or case. Predicts distribution damage before a first shipment teaches it expensively.
qs: Will the product survive our actual distribution route intact?
Does the case and pallet configuration hold under stacking?
Which packaging component fails first?
What damage rate should we budget for?

name: Environmental test
what: Exposure to temperature, humidity, light, salt or dust extremes for a defined duration, checking function and appearance afterwards. Relevant for outdoor products, food in unrefrigerated retail and export markets.
qs: Does the product survive the climate conditions it will meet?
Does appearance, colour or seal degrade under exposure?
Which storage conditions must be specified to retailers?
Is performance stable across the seasonal range?

name: Accelerated aging test
what: Elevated temperature, humidity or light is used to compress months of aging into weeks, with results extrapolated to real shelf life. Fast and cheap, but the extrapolation must later be confirmed by real-time data.
qs: What shelf life does the product plausibly achieve?
Which attribute degrades first over time?
Does the packaging protect adequately over the claimed life?
Is our date-marking claim defensible?

name: Assembly test
what: The product is assembled repeatedly by representative people — customers or line staff — with time, errors and instruction failures recorded. Directly predicts returns, support load and labour cost.
qs: Can the target person assemble it correctly without help?
How long does assembly take, and where do errors occur?
Which instruction step is misread?
Which design change would remove the most assembly time?

name: Cleanability test
what: The product or equipment is soiled in a realistic way, cleaned by the intended method, and inspected for residue, damage and time taken. Critical for foodservice equipment, reusable packaging and anything in a professional kitchen.
qs: Can it be cleaned to the required standard by the intended method?
How long does cleaning take in a real shift?
Does repeated cleaning damage the product?
Are there areas where residue accumulates?

name: Storage test
what: Products are stored under realistic conditions and configurations — stacked, in a chiller, in a shop backroom — and checked over time for damage, deformation, seal integrity and appearance. Also tests whether the format fits customers' real storage space.
qs: Does the product hold up under real storage conditions?
Can it be stacked and stored as our logistics assume?
Does it fit the space customers actually have?
How does appearance change over the storage period?

name: Usability test
what: Representative users attempt realistic tasks with the product while being observed, thinking aloud, with no help given. The core method for finding where a product fails people rather than fails technically.
qs: Can target users achieve the core task unaided?
Where do they hesitate, err or give up?
Which parts of the design are misinterpreted?
Which usability problem occurs across most participants?

name: Task-completion test
what: A usability test scored on a single binary outcome: did the user complete the task successfully, unaided, within a defined limit. Produces a comparable number across versions and releases.
qs: What share of users complete the core task successfully?
Does completion clear our acceptance threshold?
Which task in the flow has the lowest completion rate?
Did the redesign improve completion?

name: Time-on-task test
what: The time taken to complete defined tasks is measured across users and versions. Central where speed is the value — service throughput, kitchen prep, equipment changeover — or where slowness signals confusion.
qs: How long does the task take in practice?
Is the product faster than the current alternative?
Which step consumes the most time?
Does time improve with repetition, and how quickly?

name: Error-rate test
what: Errors are counted and classified by type and severity during realistic use, distinguishing recoverable slips from consequential mistakes. Used for safety-relevant products and for operational procedures.
qs: How often do users make errors, and which kind?
Which errors have real safety or cost consequences?
Can users detect and recover from their own errors?
Which design change removes the most frequent error?

name: First-use test
what: The very first encounter with a product is observed from unopened package to first successful use, without any prior explanation. First-use failure is a common driver of returns and one-star reviews.
qs: Does a first-time user reach success without help?
How long does time-to-first-success take?
Which step in the first experience causes abandonment?
What do users need to be told that the pack does not say?

name: Instruction-following test
what: Users are given only the written or pictorial instructions and observed as they attempt the task. Tests the documentation rather than the product, and usually finds that steps assumed obvious are not.
qs: Are the instructions sufficient without any verbal help?
Which step is misread or skipped?
Do pictures alone carry the meaning across languages?
Which warning or caution goes unnoticed?

name: Teach-back test
what: After a demonstration or reading, the user explains or demonstrates the procedure back in their own words. It exposes gaps between what was communicated and what was understood, and predicts training effort.
qs: Did the user actually understand the procedure?
Which part is consistently misunderstood?
How much training time does correct use require?
Can a trained user teach the next person?

name: Accessibility test
what: Use is tested with people who have relevant limitations — reduced vision, dexterity, strength, mobility, or limited language — as well as against applicable standards. Widens the addressable market and reduces legal risk.
qs: Can people with relevant impairments use the product or premises?
Which barriers exclude part of our intended customer base?
Do we meet the applicable accessibility requirements?
Which fix removes the largest barrier for the least cost?

name: Competitive usability test
what: The same tasks are performed on our product and on competitors' by the same users, with completion, time and errors compared side by side. Turns usability from an absolute into a relative claim.
qs: Is our product easier to use than the incumbent?
On which task are we clearly worse?
Which competitor design convention do users expect?
Is the usability gap big enough to be a selling point?

name: Home-use test (HUT)
what: Products are placed in participants' homes for a defined period and used normally, with structured feedback captured during and after. Standard in food and household goods because it captures real preparation, portions, occasions and household reactions.
qs: Does the product perform in real household conditions?
How is it actually prepared, portioned and served?
Do other household members accept it?
Would the household buy it again after the trial?

name: In-home observation
what: Direct observation of the product in use at home, rather than relying on the participant's later report. Reveals substitutions, shortcuts and storage realities that self-reports omit.
qs: How is the product really used, step by step, at home?
Which instructions are ignored in practice?
Where is it stored, and does that affect use frequency?
What does the household improvise around it?

name: Extended-use trial
what: The product is used continuously over weeks or months to reveal effects that short tests miss — wear, boredom, taste fatigue, habituation, maintenance burden. The main defence against novelty-effect false positives.
qs: Does usage hold up after the novelty passes?
Which durability or maintenance issue emerges over time?
Does satisfaction rise or fall with familiarity?
At what point do users stop, and why?

name: Repeated-use test
what: A focused version of extended use, measuring performance and satisfaction across a defined number of repeated cycles — washes, uses, servings, sessions. Directly relevant to reusables and consumables.
qs: Does performance hold over the claimed number of cycles?
At which cycle does quality visibly degrade?
Does the user's rating change between first and tenth use?
Is our durability claim defensible?

name: Longitudinal cohort test
what: A defined group is followed over an extended period with repeated measurement, so that retention, frequency and lifetime behaviour can be observed rather than estimated. Slow, but the only honest source of repeat-rate data.
qs: What share of customers are still buying after three, six, twelve months?
How does purchase frequency change over time?
Which early behaviour predicts long-term retention?
What is the realistic customer lifetime value?

name: Product diary
what: Users log each use of the product with context, quantity and satisfaction over a period. Gives frequency and occasion data that underpins consumption rates, pack sizes and repeat-purchase forecasts.
qs: How frequently is the product used in a normal week?
On which occasions and with what accompaniments?
How fast is a pack consumed, and does the size fit?
Does frequency decline over the logging period?

name: Usage-frequency test
what: A targeted measurement of how often the product or service is used per period, by observation, log data or till records. Converts vague interest into a consumption rate that revenue models depend on.
qs: How many times per month does a typical customer use or buy?
Which segment uses most often?
Does frequency justify the assumed revenue per customer?
What would raise frequency by one occasion per month?

name: Misuse testing
what: The product is deliberately used incorrectly in ways a real customer plausibly might — wrong tool, wrong setting, wrong food, children present — and the consequences recorded. Feeds warnings, design safeguards and liability assessment.
qs: How is the product likely to be misused in practice?
What happens when it is, and is anyone at risk?
Which safeguard or warning is required?
Does foreseeable misuse create liability exposure?

name: Substitution test
what: Measures how substitutable our product really is, in one of two directions. Variant A: customers replace their current product with ours for a period and are then free to choose — the switch-back rate is the measurement. Variant B: our product is removed from or added to a real assortment and what customers buy instead is observed, which quantifies how much demand is genuinely incremental rather than cannibalised.
qs: Will customers actually replace their current product with ours?
How many switch back once free to choose?
Which attribute of the incumbent do they miss?
Is our advantage strong enough to break an existing habit?

name: Informal bench tasting
what: A quick, unblinded tasting of recipe or formula variants with the team, suppliers or a few customers, run at the bench during development. Fast directional input for iteration; too biased to be used as evidence of market acceptance.
qs: Which recipe variant is worth taking into a proper test?
Is the difference between iterations perceptible at all?
Which attribute needs the next round of work?
Has the last change improved or damaged the product?

name: Expert sensory panel
what: A small panel of screened and trained assessors evaluates the product against defined sensory attributes under controlled conditions. They report what is perceptibly there, not whether they like it — liking must be measured separately with consumers.
qs: Which sensory attributes objectively characterise our product?
Are there off-notes or defects a consumer panel would not name?
Is the product sensorially distinguishable from the benchmark?
Which attribute has drifted between batches?

name: Descriptive analysis
what: A trained panel quantifies the intensity of each defined attribute on calibrated scales, producing a full sensory profile that can be plotted and compared over time. The reference method for product specification and reformulation control.
qs: What is the complete sensory profile of our product?
Where does it differ, attribute by attribute, from the target or competitor?
Which attribute changed after the reformulation?
Which profile do our best-performing variants share?

name: Acceptance test
what: A sample of target consumers rates overall liking and attribute liking, usually on a hedonic scale, under controlled serving conditions. Measures whether the product is liked, not whether it is preferred over another.
qs: Do target consumers like the product on an absolute basis?
Does overall liking clear the category norm we set?
Which attribute drags liking down?
Does liking differ by age, region or usage segment?

name: Preference test
what: Consumers taste two or more products and state which they prefer overall. Simple and decisive, though it says nothing about whether either product is liked in absolute terms.
qs: Which product do consumers prefer overall?
Is the preference share significantly different from chance?
Do sub-segments split in their preference?
Do we beat the market leader in a straight comparison?

name: Paired preference test
what: The strict two-product form of the preference test, with balanced serving order, forced choice and a statistical read against the 50/50 null. The standard method for benchmark comparisons.
qs: Do we beat the reference product in a head-to-head choice?
Is the preference split statistically meaningful at our sample size?
Does serving order affect the outcome?
Is the preference stable across repeat sessions?

name: 9-point hedonic test
what: Liking is rated on the classic nine-point scale from dislike extremely to like extremely, giving a comparable score against category norms and history. The workhorse acceptance measure in food development.
qs: What is the mean liking score, and does it beat our benchmark?
What share of tasters score 7 or above?
How does the score compare with the incumbent product?
Which variant scores highest across the whole sample?

name: Just-about-right (JAR) test
what: Consumers rate individual attributes as too little, just about right, or too much, showing the direction as well as the size of a formulation problem. Directly actionable for reformulation because it tells you which way to move.
qs: Is sweetness, salt, spice or texture at the right level for the target?
Which attribute is furthest from just-about-right?
How much liking is lost through each attribute deviation?
Do segments want different intensity levels?

name: Purchase-intent sensory test
what: A tasting followed by a purchase-intent question, usually with price shown, linking sensory performance to a commercial decision. Bridges the gap between 'tastes good' and 'would buy'.
qs: Would tasters buy this product at the intended price?
Does liking translate into stated purchase intent?
Which attribute drives the intent to buy?
How does intent change when the price is revealed?

name: Branded taste test
what: The same tasting run with full brand, pack and price visible, so the total experience is measured as the customer will meet it. Differences from the blind result quantify the brand effect.
qs: How does the product perform with all brand cues present?
Does the branding lift or depress the sensory verdict?
Does the pack set expectations the product cannot meet?
Which brand cue changes the perception most?

name: Blind vs branded comparison
what: The blind and branded results for the same products are compared directly, isolating how much of the verdict comes from the product and how much from the brand. Tells you whether to invest in the recipe or the identity.
qs: How much of our performance is product and how much is brand?
Does our brand add or subtract perceived quality?
Would a better recipe or a better brand move the number more?
Does the competitor beat us only because of their brand?

name: Triangle test
what: Assessors receive three samples, two identical and one different, and must identify the odd one out. The standard discrimination test for whether a change is perceptible at all.
qs: Can consumers detect the difference after our ingredient change?
Is the cheaper supplier's input perceptibly different?
Did the process change alter the product perceptibly?
Can we reformulate without anyone noticing?

name: Duo-trio test
what: A labelled reference is given first, then two samples, one of which matches it. Slightly easier for assessors than a triangle test and useful when a clear reference product exists.
qs: Is the new batch perceptibly different from our reference standard?
Can assessors match the variant to the control?
Does the substitution preserve the reference character?
Is the difference detectable by untrained consumers?

name: Same/different test
what: Pairs of samples are presented and assessors judge simply whether the two are the same or different. Robust and easy to run with untrained panels, at the cost of statistical power.
qs: Do consumers perceive these two batches as the same product?
Is the process variation within the perceptible range?
Is our copy of a benchmark product perceived as equivalent?
Does storage change perceived identity?

name: Paired difference test
what: Two samples are compared on one specified attribute — which is sweeter, firmer, saltier — rather than on overall difference. Targets a single formulation variable precisely.
qs: Is variant A perceptibly sweeter, firmer or saltier than variant B?
Did our reduction move the attribute detectably?
How large a change is needed before it is noticed?
Which direction did the process change push the attribute?

name: Ranking test
what: Several samples are placed in order on one attribute or on overall liking. Efficient for screening a set down to a shortlist before more precise testing.
qs: Which samples rank highest on the attribute of interest?
Which variants can be eliminated from the set?
Is the ranking consistent across assessors?
Does the ranking match our internal expectation?

name: Tetrad test
what: Four samples, two of each of two products, are sorted into two groups of two. More statistically powerful than the triangle test for the same number of assessors, so it needs fewer people.
qs: Is the difference detectable with a smaller, more powerful test?
Can we confirm a borderline triangle-test result?
Is the ingredient substitution perceptible at high confidence?
How large is the perceptual distance between the two products?

name: Category appraisal
what: A broad sensory mapping of many products in a category, profiled together, to locate white space and the sensory positions competitors occupy. Strategic rather than tactical.
qs: What sensory territory does the category currently cover?
Which sensory space is unoccupied?
Where does our product sit in the category map?
Which sensory positions correlate with market success?

name: Competitive benchmark tasting
what: Our product is tasted directly against named competitor products under controlled conditions, blind, with the same measures applied to all. The direct answer to 'are we good enough to compete'.
qs: How do we score against the specific competitors we will face?
Which competitor beats us and on which attribute?
Is our product at least at parity with the market leader?
What would it take to close the gap?

name: Attribute gap analysis
what: Profile and liking data are combined to identify which attributes explain the gap between our product and the best performer, and how much liking each gap costs. Turns sensory data into a prioritised reformulation brief.
qs: Which attribute gaps explain our liking deficit?
Which single change would gain the most liking?
Which gaps are irrelevant to consumers?
Where are we already at or above the benchmark?

name: Sensory threshold test
what: The lowest concentration at which an ingredient becomes detectable or recognisable is determined by presenting an ascending series. Used to set minimum effective and maximum acceptable levels for flavours, salt, sugar and additives.
qs: At what level does this ingredient become detectable?
What is the minimum dose that delivers the intended effect?
At what point does an off-note become noticeable?
How much can we reduce before consumers detect it?

name: Time-intensity test
what: Assessors track how the intensity of an attribute changes over the eating or drinking experience, second by second. Captures onset, peak and aftertaste, which single-point ratings miss entirely.
qs: How does flavour or texture evolve over the eating experience?
Is there an unwanted lingering aftertaste?
Does the sweetener behave like sugar over time?
Where in the profile does our product differ from the benchmark?

name: Shelf-life sensory test
what: Product stored under real conditions is tasted at intervals against a fresh control until the sensory difference becomes unacceptable. The real-time reference for a date-marking decision.
qs: How long does the product remain sensorially acceptable?
Which attribute degrades first and fastest?
Is our proposed best-before date defensible?
Does storage condition materially change the outcome?

name: Accelerated shelf-life test
what: Storage at elevated temperature or humidity compresses aging, and results are modelled back to normal conditions to estimate shelf life within weeks. Fast for development decisions, but must be confirmed by real-time data before a claim is printed.
qs: What is the estimated shelf life without waiting a full year?
Which formulation resists degradation best?
Does the packaging change extend stability?
Which failure mode drives the end of life?

name: Packaging–product interaction test
what: The product is stored in its actual packaging and checked for migration, scalping of flavour, discolouration, corrosion or seal degradation over time. Catches problems that appear only when the two are combined.
qs: Does the packaging alter the product's taste, aroma or colour?
Does the product attack the packaging or its seal?
Is there any migration risk requiring compliance work?
Does the pack maintain quality to the end of the claimed life?

name: Preparation-method test
what: The product is prepared by the different methods customers will realistically use — oven, pan, microwave, air fryer, over-cooked, from frozen — and evaluated after each. Guards against a product that only works in the developer's ideal conditions.
qs: Does the product work across the preparation methods customers use?
Which method gives the worst result, and how bad is it?
Is the product tolerant of over- or under-cooking?
Which instruction gives the most reliable outcome?

name: Serving-format test
what: Portion size, plating, vessel, temperature and accompaniment are varied to find the format in which the product performs best. Directly determines menu design, pack size and price point.
qs: Which portion size and format do customers prefer?
Does the serving vessel or temperature change the verdict?
Which accompaniment improves the experience most?
Which format supports the intended price?

name: Recipe substitution test
what: A single ingredient is replaced — a cheaper supplier, a local source, an allergen-free alternative — and the resulting product is compared to the control on both discrimination and liking. The standard cost-reduction and reformulation check.
qs: Can we substitute this ingredient without a perceptible loss?
How much cost does the substitution save per unit?
Does the substitute change shelf life or processing?
Do consumers still prefer our product after the change?

name: Formula optimization DOE
what: A designed experiment varies several formulation factors systematically so that main effects and interactions can be modelled and an optimum predicted. Far more efficient than changing one ingredient at a time.
qs: Which combination of ingredient levels maximises liking?
Which factors interact, and which can be set independently?
What is the cheapest formulation that holds acceptance?
How robust is the optimum to small process variation?

name: Sensory + instrumental correlation
what: Instrument readings — texture analyser, colorimeter, pH, viscosity, Brix — are correlated with trained-panel or consumer scores to build a model. Once validated, cheap instrument measurements can stand in for panels in routine quality control.
qs: Which instrumental measure predicts the sensory attribute we care about?
Can we replace routine panel testing with an instrument reading?
What instrument specification corresponds to consumer acceptability?
Which quality-control limits should we set on the line?

name: Open-ended WTP test
what: Customers are asked directly what they would pay for the product after seeing or experiencing it, with no anchors offered. Quick and useful for a first range, but stated willingness to pay is consistently biased and should never be the only pricing evidence.
qs: What price range do customers name unprompted?
How wide is the spread between segments?
Is our intended price inside or outside the stated range?
What reference product are they pricing against?

name: Price ladder
what: The same offer is presented at ascending or descending price points, to the same or matched groups, and purchase intent is recorded at each. Produces a simple demand curve for a single product.
qs: At which price does purchase intent start to fall away?
What is the shape of the demand curve across our range?
Which price maximises expected revenue?
Is there a price cliff, and where?

name: Gabor-Granger test
what: Each respondent is asked whether they would buy at a given price, then re-asked at higher or lower prices depending on the answer, building an individual demand curve. Gives a revenue-maximising price estimate at modest sample sizes.
qs: What share of customers would buy at each price point?
Which price maximises expected revenue per customer?
How price-sensitive is each segment?
How much volume do we lose per euro of price increase?

name: Conjoint analysis
what: Respondents choose between product profiles that vary systematically across attributes and price, and the model infers the value of each attribute level. Reveals what customers will actually trade off, not what they say matters.
qs: How much is each feature worth in money terms?
Which attribute combination maximises preference at our target price?
What premium does our differentiator actually justify?
Which features can be removed without losing preference?

name: Choice-based conjoint
what: The choice-task form of conjoint, where respondents repeatedly pick one option from a competitive set including a none option. Closest to a real purchase decision and the basis for share simulations.
qs: What market share would our configuration take against real competitors?
How does share change if we raise price by ten percent?
Which competitor do we take share from?
How many customers choose none at every price?

name: Discrete-choice experiment
what: A designed choice experiment, statistically specified, that estimates utilities and price sensitivity across a defined competitive set. The most rigorous stated-preference method, and correspondingly the most expensive.
qs: What are the estimated utilities for each attribute and price level?
What is the own-price and cross-price elasticity?
Which segments have materially different preference structures?
What is the optimal price given the competitive response?

name: Price elasticity experiment
what: Actual prices are varied in the real market — across stores, geographies or time periods — and the volume response measured. Behavioural rather than stated, and therefore much stronger evidence than any survey method.
qs: How does real volume respond to an actual price change?
What is our measured elasticity in this channel?
Does a price rise increase or reduce total contribution?
Do different locations respond differently?

name: Real-money auction
what: Participants bid real money for the product in an incentive-compatible auction format such as BDM or Vickrey, so understating or overstating their true value costs them. Produces the most credible willingness-to-pay figures short of a live sale.
qs: What will customers actually pay when the money is real?
How does true willingness to pay compare with stated?
How wide is the distribution of real valuations?
Does our intended price sit above or below the median bid?

name: Pay-what-you-want test
what: Customers set their own price, with or without a suggested anchor or floor, and the distribution of payments is recorded. Reveals perceived value and social norms; used as a launch tactic as well as a measurement.
qs: What do customers voluntarily pay when free to choose?
How does an anchor or suggested price shift the distribution?
What share pay nothing or the minimum?
Is average voluntary payment above our unit cost?

name: Sales conversation test
what: A structured live sales conversation is held with real prospects using a defined pitch, with objections, price reactions and outcomes logged. The most information-dense early sales experiment because the objections come back immediately.
qs: Can we close a real sale with this pitch?
Which objection appears most often?
Which value argument moves the prospect?
What close rate do we achieve per qualified conversation?

name: Cold outreach test
what: A defined list of prospects is contacted cold by email, phone or in person with a consistent message, and reply and meeting rates are measured. Tests both the message and whether the segment is reachable at all.
qs: What reply and meeting rate does this message achieve?
Which segment responds best to cold contact?
Which subject line or opener works?
Is this channel economically viable for acquisition?

name: Outbound offer test
what: A concrete, priced offer with a deadline is sent to a defined list, and acceptance is measured. Sharper than an outreach test because the outcome is a purchase decision rather than a conversation.
qs: Will prospects accept a specific priced offer?
Which offer structure converts best?
Does a deadline change the acceptance rate?
What is the revenue per contact for this list?

name: Sales-script A/B test
what: Two versions of the pitch — different opener, benefit order, price framing or close — are used across matched sets of prospects and compared on conversion. Isolates the effect of message rather than of salesperson enthusiasm.
qs: Which script version converts more prospects?
Does leading with price or with benefit work better?
Which objection handling reduces drop-off?
Is the difference consistent across salespeople?

name: Demo test
what: The product is demonstrated live to prospects — in store, at a trade fair, on site — and the outcome, questions and objections are recorded. Reveals whether the value is visible in a few minutes and what the demo must show.
qs: Does a live demonstration convert interest into a purchase?
Which part of the demo produces the reaction?
What do prospects ask that the demo fails to answer?
What conversion rate does a demo produce?

name: Coupon test
what: Discount coupons with distinct codes are distributed through different channels or at different discount levels, and redemption is tracked. Measures channel effectiveness and price sensitivity at once.
qs: Which channel produces the most redemptions?
What discount level is needed to trigger a first purchase?
Do coupon customers return at full price?
What is the cost per acquired customer by channel?

name: Limited-drop launch
what: A deliberately small batch is released in a short window, creating a clean measurement of how fast a defined quantity sells and at what price. Also a low-risk way to test a new variant without committing stock.
qs: How quickly does a limited quantity sell through?
What price does scarcity support?
How large is the demand overhang after sell-out?
Which variant sells out first?

name: Waitlist-to-purchase conversion
what: The people who joined a waitlist are asked to buy, and the conversion rate from list to paid order is measured. It calibrates how much a sign-up is really worth and corrects over-optimistic list-based forecasts.
qs: What share of waitlist members actually buy when asked?
How does conversion decay with time since sign-up?
Which acquisition source produces the best converting list members?
What revenue can we forecast per thousand sign-ups?

name: Repeat-purchase test
what: Whether and how quickly first-time buyers buy again is tracked over a defined window. For consumables and hospitality this is the single most important commercial number, and it cannot be estimated from satisfaction scores.
qs: What share of first-time buyers purchase again within the window?
What is the average time between first and second purchase?
Which product or segment repeats best?
Is the repeat rate high enough for the business model to work?

name: Referral test
what: Existing customers are given a structured reason and mechanism to refer others, and referral and downstream conversion are measured. Run small it tests whether the product produces genuine advocacy at all; run as a full campaign with a defined incentive and message it tests whether advocacy can be organised into a repeatable acquisition channel.
qs: Do customers actually refer others when asked?
How many new customers does one existing customer generate?
Which incentive structure produces the most referrals?
Do referred customers convert and retain better?

name: Gift-purchase test
what: The product is offered and merchandised as a gift — bundle, presentation, message, seasonal timing — and gifting demand is measured separately from self-purchase. Many craft and food products earn most of their margin here.
qs: Is there meaningful demand for this as a gift?
Which format and price point works for gifting?
How concentrated is gift demand around specific seasons?
Do gift recipients later become buyers?

name: Basket test
what: What else customers buy in the same transaction is analysed from till data, to see which products travel together and what our item adds to basket value. Determines adjacency, placement and bundling decisions.
qs: What else is bought together with our product?
Does our product raise or cannibalise basket value?
Which adjacency should we be merchandised next to?
Which bundle would customers plausibly accept?

name: Market-stall test
what: A temporary staffed stall in a real trading location sells the product to real customers for a day or a weekend. The cheapest way to get genuine transaction data, live objections and price reactions in one go.
qs: Will passers-by buy at our price, and at what rate?
How many transactions per hour of footfall can we achieve?
Which objection comes up repeatedly at the point of sale?
Which variant or size sells best?

name: Farmers' market test
what: A recurring stall at a food market, run over several weeks, tests repeat custom, seasonality and word of mouth as well as first-time sales. The regular cadence makes it a real customer-acquisition and retention experiment rather than a one-off.
qs: Do customers come back week after week?
What weekly revenue can one pitch generate?
Which products drive first trial and which drive repeat?
How does weather and season affect volume?

name: Pop-up shop
what: A short-term retail space, days to a few months, trading as a real shop with real staff, stock and hours. Tests the retail concept, location, layout and economics without a long lease.
qs: Can the retail concept attract and convert real footfall?
What daily revenue and conversion rate does the location produce?
Which layout, range and price architecture works?
What are the true operating costs of a day of trading?

name: Shop-in-shop
what: A branded section inside an existing retailer's store, with our fixtures and range, trading under their footfall. Tests the concept in a real retail environment while sharing the host's traffic and overhead.
qs: Does our concept perform inside a host retailer's environment?
What sales density does our space achieve versus the host's average?
Does the host's customer profile match our target?
Are the commercial terms workable at this sales rate?

name: Consignment test
what: Stock is placed with a retailer who pays only for what sells, removing their risk and giving us clean sell-through data by store. A common route into independent retail for new food and craft brands.
qs: What is the real sell-through rate per store per week?
Which store type and location performs best?
Is the consignment margin viable for us?
Does the retailer reorder without being pushed?

name: Independent-store pilot
what: A small set of independent retailers stock the product on normal trade terms for a defined period, with sell-through, reorder and feedback tracked. Independents decide quickly, so this is the fastest real retail evidence available.
qs: Do independent retailers reorder after the first case?
What rate of sale per store per week do we achieve?
Which retailer profile suits our product?
Do trade terms leave enough margin for both sides?

name: Single-store pilot
what: The product or concept is trialled in one store, closely instrumented, to establish a baseline before any rollout. Cheap and controllable, but a single store confounds concept performance with that store's specifics.
qs: Does the concept work in a real store at all?
What baseline rate of sale should we expect?
Which operational issues appear in daily trading?
Is the result attributable to the concept or to this store?

name: Multi-store pilot
what: The same test runs across several stores of differing type, size and location, so results can be compared and store effects separated from concept effects. The step that justifies a rollout decision.
qs: Does performance hold across different store types?
How much does result vary by location and format?
Which store characteristics predict success?
Is average performance sufficient to justify rollout?

name: Geographic pilot
what: The full offer is launched in one city or region only, with marketing, distribution and operations as they would be at scale. Tests the whole system in a bounded market before national commitment.
qs: Does the full model work in a real regional market?
What penetration and repeat rate does the region reach?
What does customer acquisition cost in a real market?
Which regional factors would not transfer elsewhere?

name: Shelf-space test
what: The number of facings or the amount of shelf allocated to the product is varied across stores and the effect on rate of sale measured. Supports the space argument in a buyer negotiation with data.
qs: How much does rate of sale improve with more facings?
What is the minimum space needed to perform?
Is our sales-per-shelf-metre competitive with the incumbent?
Does extra space pay for itself?

name: Planogram test
what: Different shelf positions, blocks and adjacencies are trialled and compared on sales. Determines where in the aisle the product should sit and next to what.
qs: Which shelf position produces the best rate of sale?
Does eye-level placement justify its cost?
Which adjacency lifts sales most?
Should we be blocked by brand or by segment?

name: In-store A/B test
what: Two versions of a display, price, sign or promotion run in matched groups of stores or alternating time periods, with sales compared. Brings controlled experimentation into physical retail.
qs: Which in-store variant produces more sales?
Is the difference beyond normal store-to-store variation?
Does the promotion pay for itself in incremental margin?
Does the effect persist after the test period?

name: Sampling & sample-to-sale test
what: Free product is distributed and the subsequent purchase is tracked by code, coupon or follow-up, so that trial is measured against conversion rather than against smiles. Runs at three scales: a staffed station in store or on the street, a mass campaign through events, mailings or partner boxes, and the focused sample-to-sale measurement that attaches a tracking code to either. Measuring conversion is what separates this from a giveaway.
qs: What share of people who sample buy immediately?
What is the cost per acquired customer through sampling?
Which location and time slot converts best?
Does sampling lift store sales beyond the sampling day?

name: In-store demo
what: A live demonstration or preparation of the product in the retail environment, with sales during and after compared to baseline. Especially effective where the product needs explanation or smells good.
qs: Does a demonstration lift sales, and by how much?
How long does the uplift last after the demo ends?
Does the demo pay for its staffing cost?
Which explanation makes shoppers stop?

name: Mystery-shopping test
what: Briefed shoppers visit and buy under a defined scenario, then report on service, availability, presentation and compliance against a checklist. Used both on our own stores and on competitors.
qs: Is our concept executed as specified at store level?
How does the real customer experience compare to the standard?
Where does service or availability fail?
How do competitors handle the same scenario?

name: Competitor-store immersion
what: Structured time spent inside competitors' stores observing traffic, dwell, conversion, staffing, range and pricing. A cheap way to estimate a competitor's economics and to learn the category's operating conventions.
qs: What footfall and conversion does a comparable store achieve?
How is the competitor's range and price architecture built?
How many staff do they run and at which hours?
Which of their practices should we copy or avoid?

name: Store intercept interview
what: Short interviews with shoppers immediately after they choose or reject a product, at the point of decision. The recall is fresh and tied to a specific real decision rather than a hypothetical one.
qs: Why did this shopper choose what they chose just now?
Did they see our product at all?
What would have made them pick ours instead?
What did they expect our price to be?

name: Retailer buyer pitch test
what: A real listing pitch to a retail buyer, with the full sales story, margins, terms and support plan, and the buyer's questions and decision recorded. It tests the trade proposition, which is a different product from the consumer proposition.
qs: Will a buyer list the product on the terms we propose?
Which trade objection blocks the listing?
What margin, support and volume do they require?
Which category does the buyer file us in?

name: Distributor pitch test
what: The same exercise with distributors or wholesalers, testing whether the product fits their portfolio, logistics and margin expectations. Often the real gatekeeper for reaching independent retail and foodservice.
qs: Will a distributor take the product into their portfolio?
What margin and minimum volumes do they require?
