Can our packaging and logistics meet their requirements?
Which channel access does the distributor actually deliver?

name: Competitor dining immersion
what: Structured visits to comparable restaurants, eating the menu and recording covers, turn times, staffing, pricing, portioning and waste signals. Produces a grounded estimate of a competitor's economics and of the local standard to beat.
qs: What covers, average spend and turn time does a comparable venue achieve?
How is their menu engineered, and where is the margin?
How many staff run the service, and at what hours?
Which gap in their offer could we occupy?

name: Guided tasting
what: A hosted tasting where the concept, provenance and preparation are explained alongside the food, and reactions to both product and story are captured. Tests whether the narrative adds perceived value that supports the price.
qs: Does the story increase perceived value and willingness to pay?
Which part of the narrative resonates?
Do guests repeat the story back accurately?
Does explanation rescue a dish that fails blind?

name: Supper club
what: A ticketed meal for a small group, run in a borrowed or private space, with a fixed menu and a real price. It tests menu, pricing, service flow and word of mouth at a fraction of the cost of a venue.
qs: Will people pay a real ticket price for this concept?
Does the fixed menu work as a whole experience?
How fast do seats sell, and through which channel?
Do guests bring others to the next edition?

name: Private dinner
what: A single hosted dinner for an invited group, used to test recipes, sequencing and the concept narrative in depth with attentive feedback. Rich qualitative input, but the guests are friendly and the demand signal is weak.
qs: Does the menu work as a sequenced experience?
Which courses land and which are cut?
What do guests notice that we did not?
Is the concept coherent enough to charge for?

name: Food-truck test
what: A mobile unit trades the concept across different locations and days, testing both the offer and the effect of location. Mobility turns location itself into an experimental variable.
qs: Which locations and times generate viable volume?
What daily revenue and margin can a single unit achieve?
How does the menu need to change for speed of service?
Which pitch would justify a permanent site?

name: Catering test
what: The concept is delivered as catering for events, offices or private clients, generating revenue and operational learning with no venue cost. It also tests a distinct customer segment with different economics.
qs: Is there a viable catering demand at our prices?
What margin does catering produce compared with a venue?
Can the food travel and hold quality?
Does catering demand repeat and refer?

name: Chef's-table test
what: A small number of guests eat at or beside the pass, giving direct, immediate reactions while the kitchen observes their eating. High-fidelity qualitative feedback on plate-level decisions.
qs: How do guests actually react to each plate as it lands?
What is left on the plate, and why?
Which dish generates spontaneous comment?
What should change before the dish goes on a menu?

name: Reservation-demand test
what: Bookings are opened for dates, sittings or an unopened venue, and the rate and pattern of reservations is measured. A clean demand signal that can be run before any kitchen exists.
qs: How quickly do bookings fill for each sitting?
Which days, times and party sizes are in demand?
How large is the no-show and cancellation rate?
Does demand justify the planned capacity?

name: Ticketed-event test
what: A paid-ticket event with a defined capacity and deadline, where sell-out speed measures demand precisely. Prepayment also removes no-show risk and funds the event.
qs: How fast does the event sell out at this price?
What price point clears the capacity we planned?
Which channel sells the most tickets?
Would attendees pay for a repeat edition?

name: Menu test
what: Alternative menus — different items, structure, wording, price architecture — are trialled in real service and compared on selection mix, spend per head and margin. Menu changes are among the cheapest and highest-leverage experiments in hospitality.
qs: Which menu structure produces the highest spend per head?
Which dishes are ordered and which are ignored?
Does menu wording change what guests choose?
How many items can we cut without losing appeal?

name: Menu engineering test
what: Each dish is classified by contribution margin and popularity, and layout, pricing or recipe is changed to shift the mix toward the profitable items. A structured optimisation rather than a demand test.
qs: Which dishes are high-margin and popular, and which are neither?
Does repositioning an item on the page change its sales share?
Which item should be re-priced, re-costed or removed?
How much does the mix shift improve overall margin?

name: Service blueprint test
what: The full service is mapped into front-stage actions, back-stage actions and support processes, then walked through step by step to find failure points and handovers. Design work that precedes and structures the operational pilots.
qs: Where are the handovers and single points of failure in the service?
Which back-stage step constrains the front-stage promise?
What staffing does each step require?
Which step should be tested live first?

name: Kitchen stress test
what: The kitchen is run at or above expected peak volume, with orders fired at maximum realistic rate, to find where output, quality or timing breaks. Best done before opening rather than discovered on a Friday night.
qs: How many covers per hour can the kitchen actually produce?
At what volume does quality or ticket time break down?
Which station is the bottleneck?
What equipment or staffing change lifts the ceiling?

name: Soft opening
what: The venue trades at reduced capacity, limited menu or invited-guest volume before full opening, to shake out operations under real conditions. Both a rehearsal and a real revenue test.
qs: Does the whole operation function with real guests?
What are the actual costs and margins per cover?
Which operational failures appear under real service?
Are guests satisfied enough to return at full price?

name: Friends-and-family opening
what: The earliest trading rehearsal with a friendly, invited audience, used to test flow, timing and staff confidence with low stakes. Useful operationally, but the demand and satisfaction signals are biased and should not be counted as evidence.
qs: Does the service run end to end without breaking?
Where do staff hesitate or duplicate work?
How long does each stage actually take?
What must be fixed before paying strangers arrive?

name: Secret-shopper restaurant test
what: Briefed guests visit unannounced and score the experience against a defined standard — greeting, timing, food, cleanliness, upsell, payment. Measures consistency of execution rather than concept appeal.
qs: Is the service standard delivered consistently across shifts?
Which touchpoint fails most often?
Do staff execute the intended upsell or ritual?
How do we compare against competitors on the same checklist?

name: Business Model Canvas hypothesis test
what: Each block of the canvas is rewritten as an explicit, falsifiable assumption, ranked by risk and evidence, and the riskiest are turned into experiments. It is a planning method that produces a test agenda rather than evidence itself.
qs: Which assumptions would kill the business if they were wrong?
Which of them do we have real evidence for today?
Which assumption should be tested first, given cost and risk?
Which block of the model is least examined?

name: Unit-economics pilot
what: A small volume of real transactions is run with every cost captured — inputs, labour, packaging, waste, fees, delivery — to calculate the true contribution per unit. Almost always the moment a plan's assumed margin meets reality.
qs: What does one unit really cost to produce and deliver?
What contribution margin does a real sale generate?
Which cost line is materially larger than planned?
At what volume does the unit become profitable?

name: Small-batch production economics
what: A production batch is run at realistic small scale with time, yield, scrap and overhead measured, to establish the cost curve at the volumes the business will actually start at. Prevents planning on unreachable at-scale costs.
qs: What does the product cost at the batch size we can actually run?
How much does cost fall with each doubling of batch size?
What is the minimum batch that is economically sensible?
Which fixed cost dominates at low volume?

name: MOQ test
what: Suppliers, co-packers and printers are asked for their real minimum order quantities and the price steps around them, and the resulting working-capital requirement is calculated. It often reshapes the entire launch plan.
qs: What minimum volumes must we commit to for each input?
How much cash is locked up at the smallest viable order?
Which supplier offers the lowest entry commitment?
How many months of stock does one MOQ represent?

name: Supplier quote test
what: Formal quotes are obtained from several suppliers against the same specification, revealing real price levels, volume breaks, lead times and terms. It replaces assumed input costs with numbers you can hold someone to.
qs: What does the input actually cost at our volume?
How wide is the spread between suppliers?
At which volume does the price break?
What lead time and payment terms can we secure?

name: Manufacturing pilot
what: A trial production run on production-representative equipment, at reduced volume, to verify that the process works, the specification holds and the costing is right. The gate before committing to volume manufacture.
qs: Can the product be manufactured to specification at volume?
What yield, scrap rate and cycle time do we achieve?
Which process step is the constraint?
Is the manufactured cost within our target?

name: Contract-manufacturer pilot
what: A trial run with an external co-packer or manufacturer, testing not only the product but the relationship — communication, quality management, flexibility, changeover and true landed cost. Outsourcing risk is organisational as much as technical.
qs: Can the co-packer make our product to our specification?
What is the true landed cost including their minimums and changeovers?
How responsive and flexible are they in practice?
Which quality controls do they actually run?

name: Yield test
what: Measures how much saleable output is produced from a given quantity of input, across realistic conditions and operators. Yield assumptions are a common and quiet source of margin error in food and craft production.
qs: What is the real yield from raw input to saleable product?
How much does yield vary by batch, season or operator?
Which step loses the most material?
Does the real yield support our costed margin?

name: Waste test
what: All waste is measured across a production or trading period — trim, spoilage, overproduction, returns, breakage — and valued at cost. Turns an invisible cost into a manageable one.
qs: How much of our input value is lost as waste?
Where in the process does waste concentrate?
What does waste cost us per week?
Which change would reduce it most cheaply?

name: Labor-time study
what: Each task is timed across repetitions and operators to establish real labour minutes per unit or per cover. Labour is usually the largest and most misjudged cost in physical businesses.
qs: How many labour minutes does one unit or cover really take?
How much does time vary between operators?
Which task consumes the most labour?
Does our staffing plan match measured demand?

name: Throughput test
what: The maximum sustainable output of the system per hour or per shift is measured under realistic conditions. Establishes the capacity ceiling that the revenue model has to live within.
qs: How many units or covers can we produce per hour sustainably?
Does throughput hold across a full shift?
Which resource limits output first?
Can we meet forecast peak demand?

name: Bottleneck test
what: The constraint in the process is identified by loading the system and observing where queues form, then relieved and re-measured to see where the constraint moves. Iterative and often surprisingly cheap to act on.
qs: Which step actually limits our output?
How much extra capacity does relieving it deliver?
Where does the constraint move once relieved?
What is the cheapest way to raise the ceiling?

name: Margin waterfall
what: The full path from list price to net contribution is laid out step by step — discounts, listing fees, promotions, distributor and retailer margin, logistics, returns, payment fees — with real numbers at each step. Frequently shows that a nominally healthy margin is nearly gone.
qs: What actually remains of our price after every deduction?
Which deduction is largest and most negotiable?
Is the channel profitable after all costs?
What list price is needed to hit our target contribution?

name: Channel-margin test
what: The same product is sold through different channels — direct, market, independent retail, distributor, foodservice, online — with the true net margin and effort of each calculated. Decides where to focus scarce capacity.
qs: Which channel actually makes us money?
How much does the margin differ between channels?
Which channel's volume justifies its lower margin?
Where should we concentrate limited capacity?

name: Franchisee interest test
what: Potential franchisees or partners are approached with a real proposition — investment, returns, obligations — and their interest and questions recorded. Tests whether the concept is attractive to operators, which is a different market from customers.
qs: Are there qualified operators willing to invest in this concept?
What returns and support do they expect?
Which part of the proposition creates hesitation?
How much capital can a typical candidate bring?

name: Franchise prototype
what: A single unit is run explicitly as the template to be copied, with every process, spec and cost documented so it can be handed to someone else. It tests transferability, not just profitability.
qs: Can this unit be fully documented and handed to an operator?
Which parts of the model depend on the founder personally?
What training and support would a franchisee need?
Does a documented unit still hit its economics?

name: Replication test
what: A second unit, batch or site is run using only the written model, with performance compared against the original. The gap between the two measures how much of the success is systematic and how much was circumstance.
qs: Does performance transfer when the model is copied?
Which results depended on the original site or people?
What was missing from the documentation?
How long does a copy take to reach the original's performance?

name: Location pilot
what: A specific site is trialled — by pop-up, stall, truck or short-term occupation — before any long commitment, measuring footfall, catchment, conversion and takings on that spot. Location is usually the largest irreversible bet in a physical business.
qs: Does this specific location deliver the footfall and takings we need?
How does the catchment behave by day and hour?
What conversion rate does passing traffic produce?
Does the site support the rent being asked?

name: Subscription pilot
what: A recurring offer — box, membership, standing order, club — is run with a small cohort for several cycles, measuring churn, fulfilment cost and cash rhythm. Recurring models fail on retention and logistics far more often than on acquisition.
qs: Will customers commit to a recurring purchase?
What is the churn rate after the second and third cycle?
What does fulfilment cost per cycle in reality?
Does the recurring model beat one-off selling on contribution?

name: Ad concept test
what: Alternative advertising ideas — the core idea, not the execution — are tested with the target group for attention, comprehension, relevance and motivation. Cheap filter before production money is spent on the wrong idea.
qs: Which advertising idea gets attention and is understood?
Which concept motivates a next step rather than just amusing?
Is the product or benefit remembered afterwards?
Which idea is worth producing properly?

name: Paid traffic smoke test
what: A small paid campaign drives traffic to an offer page for a product that may not exist yet, measuring click-through, cost per click and conversion. Buys a fast, quantified demand read for a defined budget.
qs: Is there enough demand to make paid acquisition viable?
What does a lead or order cost at this stage?
Which audience and message combination performs best?
Is the click-to-conversion rate above our threshold?

name: Creative A/B test
what: Two or more creative executions — image, copy, format — run against the same audience with everything else held constant, compared on click and conversion. Isolates the effect of the creative alone.
qs: Which creative execution converts better?
Does product imagery or lifestyle imagery work harder?
Is the difference large enough to reallocate budget?
Which creative sustains performance rather than burning out?

name: Audience A/B test
what: The same creative is served to different audience definitions — segment, interest, geography, lookalike — and performance compared. It tests targeting rather than message, and often reveals the real customer is not the assumed one.
qs: Which audience responds most strongly to our offer?
Is our assumed target actually the best-performing one?
How much does acquisition cost differ between segments?
Which geography converts best?

name: Offer A/B test
what: Different commercial offers — price, bundle, discount, guarantee, free delivery, first-order incentive — are tested with identical creative and audience. Offer structure usually moves conversion more than creative does.
qs: Which offer structure produces the most conversions?
Is a discount or a guarantee more effective?
Does free delivery pay for itself in conversion lift?
Which offer attracts customers who then repeat?

name: Lead-generation test
what: A campaign collects qualified enquiries or bookings, and both the volume and the downstream conversion of those leads are tracked. Prevents optimising for cheap leads that never buy.
qs: What does a qualified lead cost through this channel?
What share of leads convert to a sale?
Which lead source produces the best conversion?
Is the channel economically viable at our margin?

name: Influencer seeding
what: Product is sent to selected creators or local figures without a paid obligation, and coverage, sentiment and resulting traffic are tracked. Tests whether the product is inherently interesting enough to be talked about.
qs: Do creators post about the product without being paid to?
How do they describe it in their own words?
Which creator profile generates real engagement?
Does organic coverage produce measurable traffic or sales?

name: Influencer conversion test
what: Paid creator collaborations run with unique codes or links so sales, not impressions, are attributed to each. Separates reach from commercial effect, which usually differ a great deal.
qs: Do influencer posts produce actual sales?
What is the cost per acquired customer per creator?
Which creator size and niche converts best?
Does the effect last beyond the posting day?

name: Street-intercept campaign
what: Staff approach passers-by in a chosen location with a sample, offer or short pitch, recording approach, engagement and conversion counts. Gives a hard read on how hard the offer is to sell face to face.
qs: How many people stop, engage and buy per hour?
Which pitch opens the most conversations?
Which location and time produces the best rate?
What does a customer cost through street acquisition?

name: Event activation
what: A presence at a fair, market, festival or trade show, with a defined objective and measured outcomes — samples, leads, sales, meetings. Tests both demand and the cost of reaching a concentrated audience.
qs: Does event presence generate sales or leads worth the cost?
Which event type reaches our actual buyer?
What is the cost per lead or sale at an event?
Which conversations lead to lasting relationships?

name: PR test
what: A story is pitched to media, and pickup, reach, sentiment and any resulting traffic or sales are tracked. Tests whether the venture has a story that journalists find worth telling, which is also a proxy for word-of-mouth potential.
qs: Is our story picked up by relevant media?
Which angle do journalists respond to?
Does coverage produce measurable traffic or sales?
How is the concept described by an outsider?

name: Organic content test
what: Content is published on owned or social channels and measured on reach, engagement and conversion, with different topics and formats compared. Tests whether an unpaid channel can carry acquisition before budget exists.
qs: Which content topics and formats attract our audience?
Can organic content generate customers without paid support?
What is the realistic growth rate of this channel?
Which content leads to enquiries rather than just views?

name: Competitive benchmark
what: A structured comparison of our offer against named competitors across the dimensions customers actually use — price, quality, range, convenience, service, provenance. Establishes where we genuinely stand rather than where we assume we stand.
qs: How do we compare with competitors on the criteria customers use?
On which dimension are we genuinely better?
Where are we below the category's minimum expectation?
Which competitor is the real reference point for customers?

name: Benchmark teardown
what: A competitor's product is bought, dismantled, weighed, analysed and costed component by component. Reveals their specification, likely cost structure and the engineering or recipe decisions behind their price.
qs: What is the competitor's product actually made of and what does it cost?
Where do they save cost, and where do they invest?
Which of their choices should we copy or avoid?
Can we match their specification at our volume?

name: Comparative trial
what: Customers use our product and a competitor's over a real period, in real conditions, and then report and choose. Combines the realism of a use test with the decisiveness of a direct comparison.
qs: After extended real use, which product do customers keep?
Which differences become apparent only over time?
Which competitor attribute do users miss when using ours?
Would they switch permanently?

name: Preference share test
what: A representative sample chooses among the real competitive set, and the resulting share of choice is used to estimate potential market share. More predictive than liking scores because it forces a choice against reality.
qs: What share of choices would we win against the real competitive set?
Which competitor loses share to us?
How does share change with price or distribution assumptions?
Is the potential share large enough to matter?

name: Brand switching test
what: Loyal users of a competitor are given an incentive or opportunity to switch, and the switching and switch-back rates are measured. Directly quantifies how sticky the incumbent's customers are.
qs: Will competitor loyalists switch when given the chance?
What incentive is needed to trigger a switch?
How many stay switched after the incentive ends?
Which competitor's customers are the most winnable?

name: Defection test
what: Customers who left us are studied systematically — timing, prior behaviour, stated and observed reasons — to identify the drivers and predictors of churn. Distinct from a lapsed-customer interview in that it is quantitative and cohort-based.
qs: At which point in the lifecycle do customers leave?
Which behaviours predict imminent defection?
Which cause of churn is largest by volume?
Which intervention reduces churn most?

name: “Why not?” interview
what: Short, targeted interviews with people who considered the offer and declined, focused narrowly on the reason for the no. Simple, fast and one of the highest-yield qualitative methods available.
qs: What specifically stopped this person from buying?
Is the barrier price, trust, relevance or convenience?
Which single change would have flipped the decision?
Are the reasons consistent across the people who said no?

name: Competitive positioning map
what: Competitors are plotted on the two dimensions that most drive customer choice, with our intended position marked. It clarifies whether a claimed gap is genuinely unoccupied or simply undesirable.
qs: Which position in the market is genuinely unoccupied?
Are the two axes really the ones customers decide on?
Is the gap we found empty because nobody wants it?
Which competitors would move against us if we took that position?

name: Perceptual mapping
what: Customer ratings across many attributes are reduced statistically to a map of how brands are actually perceived, rather than how their owners describe them. Grounds positioning in customer perception instead of internal opinion.
qs: How do customers actually perceive the brands in this category?
Where do we sit versus where we intend to sit?
Which attributes cluster together in customers' minds?
Which perceptual move is realistic from our current position?

name: Full customer-journey pilot
what: The complete journey is run for real customers end to end — discovery, purchase, fulfilment, use, support, repeat — with measurement at every step. It tests the whole system rather than any single component, and usually finds the breaks at the joins.
qs: Does the entire journey work end to end for a real customer?
Where do customers drop out or need intervention?
Which handover between steps fails most often?
What does serving one customer fully actually cost?

name: Service walkthrough
what: The team walks the service physically, step by step, in the real space, checking sequence, signage, timing and equipment placement before customers are involved. Cheap rehearsal that catches the obvious problems first.
qs: Does the physical sequence make sense in the actual space?
Is anything missing at the point it is needed?
Where do staff and customer paths cross badly?
Which step has no owner?

name: Role-play service test
what: Staff and colleagues play customer and server through defined scenarios, including difficult ones, to practise and to find script gaps. Focused on the interaction rather than on the space.
qs: Do staff handle the standard and difficult scenarios well?
Which situation has no script or rule?
How long does each interaction take?
Where do staff improvise inconsistently?

name: Staffing test
what: Different staffing levels and role splits are trialled across comparable periods, with service quality, throughput and labour cost compared. Establishes the minimum viable rota rather than the assumed one.
qs: What is the minimum staffing that maintains service quality?
Which role is the constraint at peak?
What does the right staffing level cost as a share of revenue?
Can roles be combined without service failure?

name: Peak-load test
what: The operation is deliberately run at maximum expected demand — a busy market day, a promotion, a booked-out service — and the failure points recorded. Capacity claims should be tested before they are marketed.
qs: Can we serve peak demand at the promised standard?
Which resource fails first under load?
How much revenue do we lose by turning people away?
What is the true maximum sustainable capacity?

name: Failure-mode simulation
what: Realistic failures are deliberately introduced — supplier misses, equipment down, staff absent, power cut, no-show — and the response observed. Preparation for the events that reliably occur in physical businesses.
qs: What happens when a key supplier, machine or person fails?
How long does recovery take?
Which failure would stop trading entirely?
Which contingency is worth putting in place?

name: Recovery test
what: A service failure is staged or a real one is followed, and the recovery process is measured on speed, cost and the customer's subsequent behaviour. Well-handled recovery often produces better retention than a flawless experience.
qs: Does our recovery process retain the customer?
What does a recovery cost per incident?
How quickly can we resolve a typical complaint?
Which recovery gesture actually restores trust?

name: Customer-support pilot
what: Support is run for real customers over a defined period, with volumes, contact reasons, resolution times and costs logged. Reveals the true support load per customer, which most plans understate.
qs: How many support contacts does each customer generate?
What are the top reasons customers get in touch?
What does support cost per customer per period?
Which product fix would remove the most contacts?

name: Return/refund test
what: The returns process is run properly — policy, logistics, inspection, restocking, refund — and rate, reason and cost per return are measured. Return economics can quietly eliminate the margin on a physical product.
qs: What is our real return rate and why do people return?
What does a return cost us fully loaded?
Can returned goods be resold, and at what value?
Does the return policy increase or decrease net contribution?

name: Delivery test
what: Real deliveries are made to real customers, measuring time, cost, damage, temperature integrity and satisfaction. For food and fragile goods the delivery step frequently determines whether the product arrives as intended.
qs: Does the product arrive intact, on time and at the right temperature?
What does a delivery really cost per order?
What damage or failure rate should we expect?
Which delivery method and packaging performs best?

name: Last-mile pilot
what: Alternative final-leg models — own courier, bike, third party, locker, pickup point — are trialled and compared on cost, reliability and customer experience. Usually the most expensive and least controllable part of physical distribution.
qs: Which last-mile model is cheapest and most reliable for us?
What is the cost per drop by method and density?
Which model gives the best customer experience?
At what order density does own delivery beat a third party?

name: Click-and-collect pilot
what: Customers order remotely and collect in person, with uptake, picking cost, wait time and add-on purchases measured. Tests a hybrid model that removes delivery cost while creating a store visit.
qs: Will customers order ahead and collect in person?
What does picking and holding an order cost?
Do collectors buy additional items on arrival?
What share of orders are collected late or not at all?

name: Specification test
what: The product is measured against its written specification, parameter by parameter, with the results documented. The formal check that what was made is what was designed.
qs: Does the product meet every parameter of its specification?
Which parameter is out of tolerance?
Is the specification itself correct and complete?
Are the measurement methods reproducible?

name: Material compatibility test
what: Materials that will be in contact — product, packaging, equipment, cleaning agents — are tested together for reaction, corrosion, migration or degradation. Particularly relevant for food contact and for reusable systems.
qs: Are the materials in contact chemically compatible?
Does any migration or corrosion occur over time?
Do our cleaning agents damage the product or equipment?
Do the materials meet food-contact requirements?

name: Safety test
what: The product is tested against the relevant safety standards and foreseeable-use risks, by an accredited lab where certification is required. Non-negotiable before sale for most physical products.
qs: Does the product meet the applicable safety standards?
Which hazards arise in foreseeable use and misuse?
Which certification is required before we can sell?
What does compliance testing cost and how long does it take?

name: Regulatory pre-check
what: The applicable rules, approvals, licences and authorities are identified and, where possible, confirmed with the authority before development goes far. Discovering a licensing barrier late is a common and avoidable way to lose a year.
qs: Which approvals, licences or registrations does this business need?
Is our intended product or premises permissible as planned?
How long does approval take and what does it cost?
Which regulatory constraint should shape the design now?

name: Label-compliance test
what: Labels and packaging are checked against the legal requirements of each target market — ingredients, allergens, nutrition, origin, weights, language, waste marks. Errors here trigger recalls and delistings.
qs: Does our label meet the legal requirements in each market?
Are allergens, quantities and origin declared correctly?
Do we have the required languages and symbols?
Which claim on the pack is legally risky?

name: Claim-substantiation test
what: Evidence is generated to support each marketing claim — organic, handmade, local, reduced sugar, durable, recyclable — to the standard a regulator or competitor would demand. Unsupported claims are both a legal and a positioning risk.
qs: Can we prove each claim we intend to make?
What evidence standard applies to this claim?
Which claim should be dropped or softened?
Is a certification needed to make the claim credible?

name: Microbiological test
what: Product and process samples are analysed for relevant organisms against defined limits, at production and across shelf life. Foundational for any food business and a prerequisite for most listings.
qs: Is the product microbiologically safe at production and end of life?
Which organisms are the critical control points for us?
Does the process reliably stay within limits?
Does shelf life hold microbiologically as well as sensorially?

name: Chemical stability test
what: Chemical parameters — pH, water activity, oxidation, acidity, active levels — are tracked over the intended shelf life and under stress. Underpins both safety and the claims made about the product.
qs: Do the key chemical parameters stay stable over shelf life?
Which degradation reaction limits the product's life?
Does the formulation stay within safe and legal ranges?
Does packaging or storage change stability?

name: Packaging integrity test
what: Seals, closures and containers are tested for leakage, seal strength, burst resistance and barrier performance, at production and after distribution. Most shelf-life failures in practice originate in the pack, not the recipe.
qs: Do the seals hold through filling, transport and shelf life?
What is the seal failure rate on our line?
Does the barrier keep out oxygen or moisture as required?
Which packaging parameter needs tighter control?

name: Tamper-evidence test
what: The tamper-evident feature is tested for whether interference is genuinely visible and whether it can be defeated and reinstated. Required in several categories and expected by retailers in more.
qs: Is tampering clearly visible to a normal customer?
Can the feature be defeated and reclosed convincingly?
Does it survive normal distribution without false triggering?
Does it meet the retailer's requirement?

name: Quality-control sampling
what: A defined sampling plan takes and tests samples across production, with limits, actions and records defined in advance. The routine system that turns one-off tests into ongoing control.
qs: Is production staying within specification over time?
What sampling frequency detects a drift fast enough?
Which parameter drifts most often?
What is the cost of the quality plan per unit?

name: Batch-to-batch consistency test
what: Multiple production batches are compared analytically and sensorially against the same standard, to quantify variation. Consistency, more than peak quality, is what retailers and repeat customers actually buy.
qs: How much do our batches vary from one another?
Is the variation perceptible to customers?
Which process variable drives the variation?
Are we consistent enough to supply a retailer?

name: Supplier qualification test
what: A supplier is assessed against defined criteria — sample testing, audit, documentation, capacity, certifications, references — before being approved. Prevents a cheap input becoming an expensive recall.
qs: Does this supplier meet our quality and documentation requirements?
Can they hold specification across repeat deliveries?
Do they have the certifications our customers demand?
What is the risk if they fail, and what is our alternative?

name: Incoming-material test
what: Each delivery of raw material is checked against specification before use, with acceptance criteria and rejection procedures defined. The first line of defence against variation entering the process.
qs: Does incoming material meet specification consistently?
How often would we have to reject a delivery?
Which input varies most, seasonally or between lots?
Does input variation explain our output variation?

name: Kitchen-to-pilot scale test
what: A recipe or process developed at bench or kitchen scale is reproduced on larger equipment, and the differences in yield, texture, timing and taste are documented. Recipes rarely survive scale-up unchanged, and this is where that is discovered.
qs: Does the recipe reproduce on larger equipment?
Which parameters must change to preserve the product?
How do yield and cost change at pilot scale?
Is the scaled product sensorially equivalent to the original?

name: Pilot-production run
what: A full run on production equipment at reduced volume, with the whole process — inputs, changeovers, quality checks, packing — executed as it would be in production. The rehearsal before commercial commitment.
qs: Can we run the full process end to end at production settings?
What throughput, yield and scrap do we achieve?
Which step is not yet production-ready?
What is the real cost per unit at this scale?

name: First-commercial-batch test
what: The first batch intended for sale is produced and monitored intensively against specification, cost and timing. It converts pilot assumptions into a commercial baseline and typically exposes the last set of surprises.
qs: Does the first saleable batch meet specification and cost?
Which problems appear only at commercial volume?
How long does a full commercial cycle take?
Is the batch fit to ship to a customer?

name: Limited geographic launch
what: The product is launched properly but only in a defined territory, with full marketing and distribution, before wider rollout. Contains the risk while producing genuine market data.
qs: Does the offer perform in a real, bounded market?
What penetration and repeat rate does the territory achieve?
What does acquisition cost at real scale?
Which results would transfer to other regions?

name: Beta launch
what: A defined group of early customers uses the product or service knowing it is unfinished, in exchange for access, price or influence. Produces intensive real-use feedback with tolerant users.
qs: Does the product work for real customers in real conditions?
Which issues do users hit that we never anticipated?
Do beta users become paying customers?
Which fixes must be made before general availability?

name: Founding-customer program
what: A small cohort of committed early customers is recruited on preferential terms in exchange for deep feedback and public support. Combines revenue, evidence and reference customers in a single move.
qs: Will customers commit early on preferential terms?
What do they demand in return?
Do they provide usable references and case material?
Do founding customers retain after the introductory terms end?

name: Ambassador program
what: Selected customers or local figures are equipped to represent and recommend the product in their own networks, with reach and conversion tracked. Tests whether advocacy can be organised rather than merely hoped for.
qs: Can advocacy be structured into a repeatable channel?
How many customers does one ambassador generate?
What motivates ambassadors beyond discounts?
Which ambassador profile performs best?

name: Launch-day stress test
what: Everything expected on the busiest day is rehearsed at full intensity — stock, staffing, systems, payment, queue, deliveries — before the real launch. A single dress rehearsal is far cheaper than a public failure.
qs: Can we handle launch-day volume without failing?
Which system or resource breaks first under launch load?
Do payment, stock and staffing hold at peak?
What contingency do we need on the day?

name: Second-location test
what: A second site is opened using the documented model from the first, and its ramp and performance compared. The decisive test of whether the business is a concept or was a single lucky location.
qs: Does the model work in a second location?
How much of the first site's success was location-specific?
How long does a new site take to reach maturity?
What does opening a second site really cost?

name: Replication across operators
what: The same model is run by different people — new staff, managers or partners — with results compared to the founder-run original. Tests whether performance depends on documented systems or on specific individuals.
qs: Do results hold when someone else runs the model?
Which parts depend on individual skill or personality?
How long does an operator take to reach the benchmark?
What training closes the performance gap?

name: Replication across customer segments
what: The offer is taken to a different customer segment with minimal adaptation, and performance compared against the original segment. Tests how far the market extends beyond the first beachhead.
qs: Does the offer work for a second customer segment?
Which adaptations does the new segment require?
Is the new segment's economics comparable?
Is the total addressable market larger than one segment?

name: International-market pilot
what: A limited launch in another country, testing not only demand but regulation, labelling, logistics, pricing, language and channel structure. Cross-border assumptions fail in more dimensions than domestic ones.
qs: Does demand exist in the target country at a viable price?
Which regulatory and labelling changes are required?
What do logistics and duties do to our landed cost?
Which local channel structure must we work through?

name: A/B test
what: Two variants are exposed to randomly assigned, comparable groups at the same time, with one primary metric decided in advance. Randomisation is what makes the difference causal rather than merely observed.
qs: Which variant performs better on the metric we chose in advance?
Is the difference statistically significant at our sample size?
Does the effect hold across the segments we care about?
Is the effect large enough to be worth implementing?

name: Multivariate test
what: Several elements are varied simultaneously across combinations, so both individual effects and interactions can be estimated. Needs substantially more traffic or volume than a simple A/B test.
qs: Which combination of elements performs best together?
Do any elements interact rather than adding up?
Which element contributes most to the outcome?
Do we have enough volume to resolve these effects?

name: Factorial experiment
what: Factors are varied at defined levels in a structured design so that all main effects and interactions can be estimated from a modest number of runs. The classic efficient design for product and process work.
qs: Which factors actually drive the outcome?
Which factors interact, and how?
What settings give the best result?
Which factors can be fixed and ignored from now on?

name: Design of experiments (DOE)
what: A family of structured experimental designs — screening, response surface, mixture — that extract the most information from the fewest runs. Standard practice in formulation, process and packaging optimisation.
qs: Which of many candidate factors matter at all?
What is the optimal setting within the feasible region?
How robust is the optimum to normal variation?
How few runs do we need to answer this reliably?

name: Sequential experimentation
what: Data is analysed as it accumulates against pre-defined stopping rules, so a test can be stopped early for success or futility. Saves time and cost, but requires the rules to be set before the test starts.
qs: Can we stop this test early with a reliable answer?
Has the variant already crossed the decision boundary?
Is the test futile and worth abandoning?
What stopping rule keeps the error rate acceptable?

name: Randomized controlled trial
what: Participants or units are randomly assigned to treatment and control and outcomes are compared, giving the strongest available causal evidence. Used in physical businesses for pricing, promotion, service and health-related claims.
qs: Does the intervention actually cause the outcome?
How large is the causal effect, with what confidence interval?
Does the effect differ between subgroups?
Would the effect persist outside the trial conditions?

name: Geo experiment
what: Whole geographies are assigned to treatment or control and aggregate outcomes compared, so effects that cannot be measured at individual level can still be estimated. The standard method for testing offline marketing and pricing.
qs: Does this marketing or pricing change lift sales in treated regions?
How large is the incremental effect against untreated regions?
Does the effect persist after the campaign ends?
What is the true return on this spend?

name: Store-level experiment
what: Stores are matched into comparable pairs or groups and assigned to test and control conditions, with sales compared over the period. The workhorse of physical retail experimentation.
qs: Does the in-store change increase sales relative to control stores?
Is the lift larger than normal store-to-store variation?
Does the effect vary by store type or region?
Does the change pay for itself in incremental margin?

name: Time-series experiment
what: The intervention is switched on and off over time in the same location, and the outcome series is analysed against the pre-period trend, controlling for seasonality. Used when no control group is available.
qs: Did the change alter the trend beyond normal variation?
How quickly does the effect appear and decay?
Is the result confounded by season, weather or events?
Does the effect reverse when the change is withdrawn?

name: Holdout test
what: A randomly selected group is deliberately excluded from an activity — campaign, offer, programme — so the true incremental effect can be measured against them. The honest measure of whether spend creates anything that would not have happened anyway.
qs: How much of the outcome is genuinely incremental?
Would these customers have bought anyway?
What is the real return on this activity?
Which segment shows the largest incremental response?

name: Cohort experiment
what: Groups defined by when they joined or which condition they entered under are tracked over time and compared on retention, frequency and value. Separates genuine improvement from changes in customer mix.
qs: Do newer cohorts retain better than older ones?
Did the change improve long-term behaviour or only first purchase?
How does customer value develop over the first year?
Which acquisition source produces the best cohorts?

name: Sequential price experiment
what: Prices are changed in a planned sequence over time and the volume and revenue response measured at each step, with seasonality controlled. A practical way to find a price curve when parallel testing is impossible.
qs: How does demand respond as we step the price up or down?
Which price maximises contribution in practice?
Do customers notice and react to repeated price changes?
Is the elasticity stable across the year?
